extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in humor theory (psychology, philosophy, linguistics)
extracted.subtask_description: A concise survey of major theoretical accounts that explain why people find things funny, describing proposed mechanisms, necessary conditions, and representative examples and proponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter serves as release of psychological tension and pent-up emotions; humor reduces psychological stress and allows expression of suppressed desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains laughter as a homeostatic mechanism. Examples: tickling produces laughter due to tension buildup and release. Figures associated: Herbert Spencer, Sigmund Freud, Immanuel Kant. Use when analyzing jokes that relieve anxiety, social inhibition, or pent-up affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises from feeling superior to others, especially when witnessing their misfortunes or inferiorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes describes laughter as 'sudden glory' from recognizing one's power over a target. Variant: Affective Disposition Theory — audiences find humor funnier when bad things happen to disliked people. Figures: Hobbes, Plato, Aristotle. Use when evaluating humor that targets social inferiority, blunders, or misfortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor results from violation of expectations via unexpected twists, contradictions, or surprising juxtapositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant: comedy as 'the sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing.' Example joke: 'What is black and white and red all over? A newspaper!' — works through unexpected word-meaning shift. Figures: Hutcheson, Schopenhauer, Beattie, Bergson. Apply to analyses that focus on surprise, mismatch, or cognitive reappraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign Violation Theory (BVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three conditions must be met for something to be funny: (1) it threatens how the world 'ought to be', (2) the threatening situation seems benign, and (3) a person sees both interpretations at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed by Peter McGraw and Caleb Warren. Use BVT to evaluate instances where norm-violation is perceived but simultaneously judged as harmless or acceptable; all three conditions are required per the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script-Based Semantic Theory of Humor (SSTH)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words or situations activate two opposing semantic scripts simultaneously; a joke requires text compatible with two different, opposite scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The joke must be compatible with both scripts and those scripts must be opposed. Example: 'Is the doctor at home?' triggers both DOCTOR and LOVER scripts. Theorist: Victor Raskin (1985). Use when analyzing verbal jokes hinging on script ambiguity and switch.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Theory of Verbal Humor (GTVH)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal humor arises from six hierarchical knowledge resources: (1) Script Opposition, (2) Logical Mechanism, (3) Situation, (4) Target, (5) Narrative Strategy, (6) Language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The six resources work hierarchically to explain how jokes are constructed and how variants relate. Theorists: Raskin, Attardo. Use GTVH for systematic analysis of joke components: what concepts oppose, how they are connected, who/what is targeted, the format, and wording choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer Model of Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor involves rapid deletion of false interpretations from consciousness, releasing excess neural energy and strengthening circuitry for detecting mistaken reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes a cognitive/neural mechanism: deleting incorrect interpretations releases energy and improves problem-solving circuitry. Theorists: Suslov (1992); Hurley, Dennett, Adams (2011). Use for theoretical or computational accounts linking perception, interpretation, and neural processing of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misattribution Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences misidentify why they find something amusing, attributing laughter to innocent elements while actually responding to taboo or hostile content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to Freud's distinction between tendentious and non-tendentious humor. Theorists: Freud, Zillmann & Bryant. Use when explaining cases where surface features seem benign but deeper motives (taboo, aggression) drive amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual Selection Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor functions as a signal of intelligence and other desirable traits, having evolved through sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated with Geoffrey Miller. Use for evolutionary accounts emphasizing mate choice and signaling; evaluates humor's role in attractiveness and cognitive fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontic–Epistemic Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises when social reality is recognized as suddenly appearing unreal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorist: P. Marteinson (2006). Apply to analyses emphasizing changes in perceived reality or the sense that familiar social structures momentarily lose their normal meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bergson's Mechanistic Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic stems from rigidity or mechanical behavior applied to living beings; 'the source of the comic is not ugliness but rigidity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorist: Henri Bergson. Use when assessing humor based on mechanical repetition, stiffness, or lack of adaptability in characters or behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense Mechanism Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor operates as a high-level psychological defense mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorist: George Eman Vaillant. Use in clinical or psychoanalytic readings where humor protects ego functioning or helps cope with stress.

rubrics_metrics.name: O'Shannon Model
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor production involves four interactive elements: context, information, aspects of awareness, and enhancers/inhibitors; jokes need not rely on high incongruity if they trigger superiority, relief, aggression, or identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorist: Dan O'Shannon (2012). Use when analyzing multifactorial interactions in joke reception; highlights alternative mechanisms (superiority, relief, aggression, identification) beyond incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex Systems Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor emerges from interacting parts in complex dynamic systems rather than from a single linear mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorists: Tschacher & Haken, Demjén. Use for systemic approaches that model humor as arising from dynamic interactions across cognitive, social, and contextual components.
